name: Pancragen

lead: Pancragen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia, aimed at pancreatic tissue.
Studies cover cell cultures, rats, monkeys and a single small human report on glucose metabolism. None address appearance.

paras: Its developers report that it raises expression of pancreatic cell differentiation factors in culture, which they propose underlies metabolic effects.
Human safety data are very limited, and it is not an approved drug in Western countries.

lead: Pancragen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp, usually amidated) developed by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, designed to target pancreatic tissue [1]. It belongs to the short synthetic peptide bioregulators the group proposes as tissue-specific regulators in ageing [1].

Research includes cell cultures showing that it raises expression of differentiation factors in pancreatic cells [2][2], streptozotocin-diabetic rats [3], aged rhesus monkeys [4][5] and one small study in older people with and without type 2 diabetes [6]. The human study reported lower fasting glucose and insulin resistance index in treated patients [6].
It is not an appearance product. Nearly all published work comes from the developing group.
infobox: Cell culture, rats, monkeys, one small human study
Not an approved drug in Western countries

paras: A 2011 study examined 30 healthy older persons and 33 older patients with type 2 diabetes. Nocturnal melatonin production was about 70 percent lower in patients than in healthy people, and in patients given Pancragen, fasting glucose, glucose tolerance test values, insulin and insulin resistance index fell, while untreated patients showed no such changes [6]. The study was small, and independent replication is not documented.

In cultured pancreatic cells, Pancragen raised expression of differentiation factors for acinar and islet cells, with effects reported in both young and aged cultures; the authors suggested this could underlie anti-diabetic and anti-inflammatory effects [1][2]. Related work found tissue-specific stimulation of CXCL12 and Hoxa3 in pancreatic cell cultures [2].

In rats with streptozotocin-induced diabetes, oral Pancragen produced a hypoglycaemic effect and intramuscular administration normalised capillary adhesion, without changing capillary permeability [3]. Russian reports described correction of impaired glucose tolerance and effects on endocrine pancreatic function in old rhesus monkeys [4][5]. Tissue-specific effects of peptides in organ cultures from young and old rats were also reported [7].
Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, describes the peptide as a synthetic analogue of a natural tetrapeptide from bovine pancreas, with studies appearing from the mid-2000s [8].
